name: Pronominal Noun Phrase

1.definition: Anaphoric reference - refers back to a previously mentioned entity (antecedent)
1.details: The interpretation can recover an earlier linguistic antecedent in the same sentence or the surrounding discourse.

2.definition: Cataphoric reference - refers forward to an entity mentioned later in the discourse
2.details: A following antecedent is possible in suitable structural and discourse settings.

examples.form: Before [he] entered the room, John switched off his phone.
examples.note: 'He' refers forward to 'John' in this reading.

3.definition: Exophoric reference - refers to an entity in the extralinguistic context (situation, shared knowledge)
3.details: Salience in the situation can identify the referent without any antecedent expression.

examples.note: Said about someone not present, referring to a shared understanding of who 'he' is.

4.definition: Bound variable reference - refers to an entity whose referent varies depending on a quantifier
4.details: The value can vary with the quantified antecedent.

examples.note: 'they' refers to each student, and its referent varies with each student.

5.definition: Dummy pronoun - has no referential meaning, serves a grammatical function
5.details: Dummy it and there occupy grammatical positions without identifying entities.

examples.note: 'It' does not refer to anything; it's a grammatical placeholder.
'There' does not refer to a place; it introduces the existence of something.

constraints.description: Must consist of a pronoun functioning as the head of the NP

relatedConstructions.notes: Traditional 'indefinite pronouns' (everybody, something, nobody) are compound determinatives in fused determiner-head function, not pronouns

projection.target: They and them can pick up a prior referent but change realization with subject versus object function. Dummy it can fill a subject slot with no antecedent, so antecedence is neither necessary for pronominal NP status nor sufficient to pick its case.
projection.evidence: CGEL separates pronominal form and syntax from anaphoric, deictic and dummy uses.

curious.title: Words that stand in for a noun phrase
curious.summary: A pronoun like he, they or it can take the place of a whole noun phrase and still work as the subject or object.
curious.body:
In John arrived. He looked tired, the word he points back to John. In Before he entered the room, John switched off his phone, he can point forward to John. Said about someone who isn't there, He's late again points to a person the speakers both know about.

Some uses point to a different person for each case: in Every student thinks they are smart, they follows each student. And in It is raining, the word it doesn't point to anything. It just fills the spot a subject normally fills.

examples.text: Before [he] entered the room, John switched off his phone.

curious.try: Find a sentence with it and ask whether the word it points to anything. What does it stand for in It is raining?

teacher.summary: Covers the different ways a pronoun NP finds its meaning, from earlier and later mentions to the situation and dummy uses.
teacher.explain: A pronominal NP consists of a pronoun as head. The dictionary distinguishes anaphoric uses (He looked tired, pointing back to John), cataphoric uses (Before he entered the room, John switched off his phone), exophoric uses (He's late again, with the referent supplied by the situation), bound variable uses (Every student thinks they are smart) and dummy uses (It is raining; There is a problem), where the pronoun doesn't identify an entity. Having an antecedent is neither necessary for pronominal NP status nor sufficient to pick its case: they and them can pick up a prior referent but change form with subject versus object function. In this grammar, everybody, something and nobody are compound determinatives, not pronouns. The dictionary marks this account as provisional.
teacher.terms: Anaphora, cataphora and exophora are the usual names for pointing back, forward and out to the situation. Dummy it is sometimes called expletive it. Indefinite pronouns is the traditional name for everybody, something and nobody, which this grammar treats differently.

examples.text: Before [he] entered the room, John switched off his phone.

watch_for: A learner might assume every it points to a thing, including the it in It is raining.
A learner might think a pronoun has to follow the noun phrase it points to, when it can point forward.
teacher.activity: Give students short texts with highlighted pronouns. They draw an arrow to what each one points to, or write "nothing" for dummy uses.

child.hook: In "It is raining", what does "it" stand for?
child.explain: Words like he can take the place of a name. In John arrived. He looked tired, he means John. In It is raining, it doesn't mean anything. It just fills the spot.
child.play: Read a short story aloud. Every time you hear he or she, point to the person it means. Does every it point to something?

checked.note: Fixed: child explanation no longer defines every pronoun as standing in for a name or noun phrase (dummy it does not); play task limited to he and she, since the entry gives they a bound-variable use. Dismissed: none.

cite: Reynolds, Brett, ed. 2026. "Pronominal Noun Phrase." English Constructionary. https://brettreynolds.ca/constructionary/linguist/np-pron-001/ (snapshot 2026-11-19, fa37529).
